doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Race in Los Angeles, Terry Pollard's quartet and the 1957 Birdland All-Stars tour
summary: He hired the best players regardless of color and saw segregation on a largely black package tour.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: When you went out to Los Angeles. What was the scene between black and white musicians like at that point?

You know it’s a weird thing. Let me first use a line that Dick Cavett said, “I’d never look” — before I say this Dick Cavett once had Lester Maddox on his show. You know Lester Maddox who was a mayor in Alabama?

He was a bigot. An out and out bigot. He had him on the show and Lester was saying to Dick Cavett he says, “Wait a minute” he says, “I’m not prejudiced at all, not at all, I don’t see any difference between black and white.” So Dick says, “You’d better buy a pair of glasses because there’s a big difference between black and white.” I never looked at it as color. I wanted the best musicians in my band. Because where I lived on the east coast, I went out with the quartet I had was Terry Pollard for four years, I had the same musicians most of the time. I had two — and Terry Pollard was a girl, a young black girl. Going on the road, they wanted to kill me, they thought it was my wife. I never looked at it that way. I just got the best players I could get. I want the best players. I’m only as good as what’s behind me. The race scene, let’s face it, it was bad all over. Even the music. It was bad not for the — amongst the musicians, but the audience — not even the audience. They came to see you, once you got off the stage and walked on the street it was probably bad. Oh yeah. Of course I traveled with a whole black show. The biggest show I’d ever been in with my life, and I got to see how bad it was. It was called the Birdland All-Stars of 1957. Headliners — listen to this show, you won’t believe this one show — Billy Eckstine, in his heyday, and he had a trio with, I forget the three guys, that famous guy, oh Bobby Tucker on piano, and whoever he had playing bass and drums. Sarah Vaughan.

And she had Jimmy Jones playing piano, Roy Haynes playing and Richard Davis. So that’s that trio. Count Basie band with Joe Williams. Now this is one show. Count Basie and Joe Williams. Phineas Newborn’s trio. Bud Powell’s trio. Lester Young’s trio. Zoot Sims, Chet Baker’s group and Jeri Southern. That was one show. But then unfortunately Chet Baker’s band, they all got busted. After we were out about three days Jeri Southern got fired because she was half drunk all the time and soon had other commitments. So I was the only white person on the whole show. And I saw how bad it was for black people, not only with white people down south but the black people weren’t good to the guys. They’d rip them off at the hotels because you couldn’t get them to stay anywhere, they’d rip off the black guys just like a white guy would, you know. It was bad. But amongst us, we had a lot of fun. I mean but it was great, I learned a whole new experience because everybody’s got their own culture. I love ethnic humor. I love sick humor. Anything dumb and sick, I could never, you can use those words today, calling each other what black people called you. In those days you could if you were in the thing. For some reason with young people it’s more offensive. But amongst the guys it’s something else.
